newsitem.title: USA: Clinton denies wrongdoing on White House guests.
newsitem.headline: Clinton denies wrongdoing on White House guests.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Wednesday suggested there was no reason for an independent counsel to investigate his White House invitations to campaign donors, saying there was no "legal issue" involved.

Clinton said he would not comment on whether a special prosecutor should investigate fund raising in last year's election campaign but he hinted he did not think it was needed on the specific matter of his asking contributors to the White House.

"I'm not going to comment. ... It is a decision that should be made strictly on the law by the attorney general not based on any politics," Clinton told a news conference when asked if an independent counsel should be appointed.

"But the evidence that we made clear yesterday -- I think that I've answered the questions about that and I don't think that there's a legal issue there," he added during a joint news conference with Chilean President Eduardo Frei.

The evidence in question was a stack of documents released by the White House on Tuesday that provided a detailed look at White House involvement in the Democratic Party's frenzied effort to raise money before the 1996 presidential election.

Buried in the papers was a handwritten note from Clinton endorsing a memo from then Democratic fund-raising chief Terry McAuliffe that proposed inviting the party's top 20 supporters to breakfast, lunch or coffee with Clinton.
The memo proposed setting dates for such get-togethers with the president for big backers, listed the top 10 donors and proposed including supporters in golf or jogging outings.

An attached note in Clinton's handwriting said: "Yes pursue all 3 (goals) and promptly -- and get other names at 100,000 or more 50,000 or more." The handwritten note added: "Ready to start overnights right away."

On Wednesday Clinton said no money was solicited during events like the coffee meetings and, when asked whether the events may have skirted or crossed the lines of what was legal, replied with a flat: "No."
"Did we hope that the people that came there would support me, particularly after we got into a political season and we were doing this? Of course we did," Clinton said.

"But there was no solicitation during the events and the guidelines which I believe were made available to you also yesterday in the documents made it clear that there was to be no price tag on the events."
It is illegal to solicit political contributions at the White House.

According to a New York Times analysis of the overnight guests from 1992 to 1996, such visitors donated $10.2 million to the Democrats. The newspaper also reported on Wednesday that some Democratic fund-raisers explicitly sold invitations to White House coffees with Clinton, offering to arrange them for a price, usually $50,000 but up to as much as $100,000.
Democratic National Committee spokeswoman Amy Weiss Tobe, asked to comment on the newspaper report, said: "If it's true, it's against the DNC policy and it's inappropriate."
Clinton has become enmeshed in a spreading fund-raising controversy that even those close to him say may become a lingering problem during his second term.
"This is going to be a lot of trouble over this year for the president," George Stephanopoulos, Clinton's former senior adviser, told ABC's Good Morning America programme.

If the release of the documents, which belong to Clinton's former deputy chief of staff Harold Ickes, has given pause to the president's supporters, it has handed a political club to his gleeful opponents.

"President Clinton ... (has) turned the White House into the most expensive bed-and-breakfast in the world," said Representative Wally Herger, a California Republican. "The White House is the people's house and shouldn't be used for political purposes."
